overview: This single-page cross-reference or subject-index sheet summarizes State Department correspondence from 1931–1938 concerning radio broadcasting and wireless communications involving Japan. Its entries cover Japanese radio use for education, distribution of reports to U.S. agencies, interference by Tokyo station JYT with War Department station WTJ at Fort Shafter, propaganda broadcasts during the Sino-Japanese fighting near Wanping, Japanese shortwave programming directed toward Brazil, and overseas programs announced by the Broadcasting Corporation of Japan. The sheet points researchers to documents filed elsewhere, notably under 800.76, 793.94/8756, and 732.94/5, and ends with a continuation reference to “Sheet 3.”

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on Japanese radio and broadcasting correspondence
subfiles.about: The sheet indexes and cross-references diplomatic correspondence concerning Japanese broadcasting, shortwave propaganda, overseas programming, and radio-frequency interference between 1931 and 1938.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records an August 21, 1931 Tokyo report on radio use in Japan, subsequently transmitted to the Federal Radio Commission and Interior Department for its discussion of educational broadcasting. It also lists a War Department complaint about interference from Tokyo station JYT with station WTJ at Fort Shafter, Hawaii, and a July 14, 1937 telegram from Grew concerning Japanese and Nanjing propaganda broadcasts during fighting near Wanping. Later entries concern Japanese shortwave broadcasts honoring Brazil on Brazilian Independence Day and a Yokohama despatch enclosing the Broadcasting Corporation of Japan’s April schedule for overseas listeners. Several entries direct readers to other decimal files, and the final notation continues the index on Sheet 3.

interest: The sheet is useful as a compact map of how Japanese broadcasting questions were dispersed across several State Department decimal-file categories rather than retained together. Its entries connect domestic educational radio, a practical trans-Pacific frequency dispute, wartime propaganda during the opening phase of the Sino-Japanese conflict, and Japan’s cultural diplomacy toward Brazil. It also preserves station call signs, telegram and despatch numbers, internal routing information, and cross-references that can help historians locate the underlying documents.
